This model was manufactured in the late 19th century by anatomist Daniel John Cunningham (1850-1909) and model makers Casciani and Son of Dublin. This is one of three such models in the Harry Brookes Allen Museum collection. This model was figured in Cunningham's 'Contribution to the surface anatomy of the cerebral hemispheres' published in 1892 in Dublin. The caption describes this model as the 'head of a male child five years old'. For this study, Cunningham produced molds for 'twenty-two models of the human head, one of the orang, one of the chimpanzee, one of the baboon, two of the Macacque, and one of [capuchin monkey]'.

creator_display_ssim: R. F. Damon and Co (estab. 1850), maker
description_tsim: This is a display board comparing the jaws of various human species and a chimpanzee. It comprises five plaster casts of primate jaw bones mounted on a wooden board: chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes), Piltdown Man, Heidelberg Man (Homo heidelbergensis), Neanderthal Man (Homo neanderthalensis) and modern human (Homo sapiens). As with the other models, there are areas of light and dark shading on the Piltdown Man jaw, indicating the missing sections of the original fossil jaw. The Piltdown fossils were conclusively shown to be a hoax in 1953. They were produced by staining and modifying human and orangutan that were then planted at a dig site in East Sussex. Students of anthropology at the time would have been shown an orderly progression of morphological change, with the chin becoming less sloping and the canine teeth reducing in size. This sequence of the changing shape of hominid jaws is very neat and linear, and reflects the assumption that progress from apes to bipedal, intelligent humans was inevitable.

Plaster model of an oversized dog brain manufactured by Deyrolle of Paris. The species is described as 'Canis familiaris', the domestic dog. Part of a comparative set of eight models, comprising brains of a frog, ammocoete (lamprey larva), alligator, shark, rabbit, dog, trout, and pigeon.

description_tsim: Left subfossil temporal bone of a southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina). Broken into two pieces. The bone has been coated in wax; a museum technique of the early to mid-20th century used to stabilise fragile bones. This specimen was collected by the McCoy Society on their expedition to Bass Strait's King Island from December 1937 to January 1938. A significant population of southern elephant seals once bred on King Island but they are now locally extinct. The species was harvested for oil in the 19th century, and it took only two decades (1802-1819) of this practice to cause the extinction of this species on the island.

description_tsim: Softcover journal article of 222 pages with green card cover contained in a cardboard sleeve. Published in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Victoria 1909, Volume V, Part I, by Professor Richard Berry and research scholar A. W. D. Robertson. The bulk of the publication is comprised of over two hundred full page ‘dioptrographic’ diagrams of Tasmanian skulls, created with an apparatus devised by German anthropologist Rudolph Martin to reproduce skull morphology accurately and consistently in two dimensions. Details on where the skulls came from, the age or life history of the individual from whom they were derived, are almost totally absent – with the notable exception of Truganini.

description_tsim: Five subfossil 5th metatarsals from Tasmanian pademelon (Thylogale billardierii). In macropods (kangaroos and wallabies) the fourth toe is very large and strong, the fifth toe moderately so; the second and third are fused; and the first toe is usually missing. These bones have been coated in wax; a museum technique of the early to mid-20th century used to stabilise fragile bones. These specimens were collected by the McCoy Society on their expedition to Bass Strait's King Island from December 6th 1937 to January 26th 1938.

Potted specimen of a brown tree snake (Boiga irregularis). One of three brown tree snakes originally contained together in a large glass jar. The brown tree snake is an arboreal rear-fanged colubrid snake native to eastern and northern coastal Australia, eastern Indonesia (Sulawesi to Papua), Papua New Guinea, and many islands in northwestern Melanesia. The snake is slender, in order to facilitate climbing, and can reach up to 2 meters in length. Its coloration may also vary, some being brown, green, or even red. Brown tree snakes prey on many things, ranging from invertebrates to birds, and even some smaller mammals. It is one of the very few colubrids found in Australia, where elapids are more common.

The decision to remove University of Melbourne Bachelor of Oral Health students from face to face classes during the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic was a rapid process. This meant the complete stop to dental simulation education where foundational handpiece skills had just been taught in earlier year levels. This stop affected the more experienced year levels where these same skills are practiced in student clinical experiences which were also halted.  With an unknown period before resumption to experiential learning, the need to maintain some level of clinical dexterity became paramount.  Many students left the Dental School one day, not to return the next, leaving their handpieces (equipment) in their lockers during the COVID lockdown. Staff understood the challenge of creating dexterity skills where the main instrument is absent for many students.  Staff created a simplistic way of engaging students in handpiece dexterity through a creative means which was delivered and monitored online. This online learning tool was developed for all Bachelor of Oral Health students, using the same simplistic reinforced messages. A video example was provided which captured 'How to create a simulated handpiece from household items' and detailed the hand and finger actions required for stable and safe use of this piece of equipment.  Brenda Ryan's involvement with this online dexterity learning was the development of the initial learning activity, testing of the activity likeness to clinical practice with staff, creation of the learning example and weekly monitoring of all student's progress. Casual staff provided additional support to this learning as the feedback for students became a significant undertaking.

description_tsim: Black and white photograph of V. Krieger, H. Bettinger and H. Butler at Krieger's farewell in 1966 from the Royal Women's Hospital. Krieger holds farewell gift of a clock whilst Bettinger looks on.  Dr Vera Isabella Krieger (1901-1992) was a trailblazer in women’s health and has left an impressive legacy. Doctor of Science of the University of Melbourne. Krieger entered the University of Melbourne in 1921, graduating BSc in 1927 and MSc in 1927. In 1938 conferred for DSc In 1926 Vera Krieger became a research bio-chemist and assistant to Dr Robert Marshall-Allen, Director of Obstetrical Research and the first Professor of Obstetrics at the University of Melbourne in1929 On the 1st of May1928, Dr Krieger was appointed as the Royal Women Hospital's first clinical biochemist where she continued to work until retirement in 1968. All her work was carried out in the Biochemistry Department at the University of Melbourne by agreement with W J Young, Associate Professor of Biochemistry and W J Osbourne, the Professor of Physiology. Her research contributed to a better understanding of many serious health conditions. She helped save countless lives.  Dr Krieger was particularly interested in high blood pressure during pregnancy. She was also keen to understand spontaneous recurrent miscarriages.  Her most important work was in the field of Rhesus immunisation.

description_tsim: Two photographs, right view and left view. Stereoscopy is a technique for creating or enhancing the illusion of depth in an image by means of stereopsis for binocular vision. Originally, stereogram referred to a pair of stereo images which could be viewed using a stereoscope. Most stereoscopic methods present a pair of two-dimensional images to the viewer. The left image is presented to the left eye and the right image is presented to the right eye. When viewed, the human brain perceives the images as a single 3D view, giving the viewer the perception of 3D depth. Skiagrapher was the term used for a radiographer until the end of the First World War. In the early days, a skiagram, (or skiagraph), was the term used for a radiograph.  Alfred  George Fryett was born in 1862 in Lewisham London. After arriving Melbourne about 1893, Fryett was among the first to use X-rays in the late 1890s, assisting at the Melbourne Hospital. Fryett also worked with surgeon Fredric Dougan Bird at Clareton Hospital and with Harry Brookes Allen, Professor of Anatomy and Pathology in the University of Melbourne. In 1901 the University of Melbourne purchased X-ray equipment under the direction of Professor Allen. In 1902 Fryett was employed by Allen to prepare specimens with opaque injections and produce this collection of skigrams which display the aterirs throughout the human body. After Bird closed Claremont Hospital in 1914, Fryett returned to England and joined the R.A.M.C working as a radiographer at Lady Dudley's Hospital. The Sands and McDougall Melbourne Directories list Fryett as having his own radio-diagnostic business ," A.G. Fryett,  X-ray Department , 41 Spring St" from 1916 to 1919. In 1919 or 1920 Fryett returned to London, suffering health problems and retired in Malborough with his wife.  Fryett like many other pionerrs in this field became an x-ray ' martyr' dying in England in 1930, the result of 'carcinoma of the axillaand lung; epithelioma of hands; x-ray burns of fingers and hands'. Like other early radiographers or 'Skiagraphists', Fryett would often use his own  hands to test the strenght of x-ray beams, instead of using photometers that could easily be mislaid. credit_line_tsim: gift of Mr Alfred G Fryett
description_tsim: Alfred  George Fryett was born in 1862 in Lewisham London. After arriving Melbourne about 1893, Fryett was among the first to use X-rays in the late 1890s, assisting at the Melbourne Hospital. Fryett also worked with surgeon Fredric Dougan Bird at Clareton Hospital and with Harry Brookes Allen, Professor of Anatomy and Pathology in the University of Melbourne. In 1901 the University of Melbourne purchased X-ray equipment under the direction of Professor Allen. In 1902 Fryett was employed by Allen to prepare specimens with opaque injections and produce this collection of skigrams which display the aterirs throughout the human body. After Bird closed Claremont Hospital in 1914, Fryett returned to England and joined the R.A.M.C working as a radiographer at Lady Dudley's Hospital. The Sands and McDougall Melbourne Directories list Fryett as having his own radio-diagnostic business ," A.G. Fryett,  X-ray Department , 41 Spring St" from 1916 to 1919. In 1919 or 1920 Fryett returned to London, suffering health problems and retired in Malborough with his wife.  Fryett like many other pionerrs in this field became an x-ray ' martyr' dying in England in 1930, the result of 'carcinoma of the axillaand lung; epithelioma of hands; x-ray burns of fingers and hands'. Like other early radiographers or 'Skiagraphists', Fryett would often use his own  hands to test the strenght of x-ray beams, instead of using photometers that could easily be mislaid.  The collection of sterio skiagrams is Fryett's work in the Anatomy department, University of Melbourne from 1902 to c. 1914.

Lilian Alexander, the first female student at Trinity College and a leading surgeon, also served overseas in World War.

In 1914 the medical school celebrated its jubilee and in the New Year honours Allen was knighted. The profession presented him with his portrait by E. They had three daughters: Edith Margaret (1893-1962), a journalist, who worked on the Argus and Australasian but was best known for her cooking notes in the Herald under the pseudonym 'Sarah Dunne'; Mary Cecil (1893-1962); and Beatrice (Biddy) (1898-1972), a musician.

credit_line_tsim: Gift of Dr James Guest, 2014
description_tsim: Frederic Wood Jones (1879-1954), anatomist, naturalist and anthropologist, Head of anatomy at the University of Melbourne in 1930-1937. Wood Jones did many studies on Indigenous human remains drawn from his own departmental museum and other institutions. For example, in the 1930s he published two papers describing Australian Aboriginal foetuses for the Journal of Anatomy, based on specimens to which he had firsthand access. The origin of the second foetus is not provided, but the first was held in the Anatomy Museum, presented by Baldwin Spencer in 1912. Paradoxically, Wood Jones was a vocal champion of Aboriginal rights and was far ahead of contemporary Australian public opinion on this issue.

credit_line_tsim: Gift of Dr James Guest, 2014
description_tsim: Coloured photocopy of a sepia photograph of Frederic Wood Jones with two other men. All are holding a young swamp harrier (Circus approximans) on The McCoy Society's Expedition to Lady Julia Percy Island. Wood Jones wrote, 'The fine native swamp harrier is the dominant bird, and it breeds among the bracken ferns upon the open island plateau. On our arrival, these birds were so tame that it was possible to pick up the fully fledged young birds from their nests among the bracken; but, although they were not molested, they very soon learned all the wariness of their kind. They are the most conspicuous birds of the island and, at almost any time of the day, half a dozen or so could be seen floating above the plateau on the watch for young rabbits, penguins and mutton birds.' (The McCoy Society's Expedition to Lady Julia Percy Island. Nature 138, 906–908 (1936). https://doi.org/10.1038/138906a0)  Lady Julia Percy Island lies off the coast of western Victoria (38° 24′ S., 142° E.) The complete ecological survey of Lady Julia Percy Island was the first enterprise undertaken (in January 1936) by the McCoy Society for Field Investigation and Research.  The McCoy Society was founded and organized by students of the University of Melbourne during 1935. Frederic Wood Jones helped to found the McCoy Society for Field Investigation and Research, he became its first president and took part in its ecological surveys of various offshore islands.

Gweneth Wisewould (1884-1972), Annie Bennett (1891-1940) and Ellen Balaam (1892-1985) play croquet, with Ellen Ballam on the right about to hit the ball.  These three young women were to make a remarkable contribution to medicine in Victoria. Ellen Balaam was the first the first woman from her continuation school (now known as Mac.Robertson Girls' High School) to graduate from Medicine, and the first woman to do general surgery in Melbourne.  Annie Lister Bennett devoted her life to medicine and the community of the Goulburn Valley at Mooroopna in Victoria.  Gwen Wisewould found it exceptionally difficult to establish a practice in Melbourne and so established one in Trentham in 1938, staying for 34 years until her death in 1972.  This postcard is related to four other images taken at the same time: MHM2014.17, MHM2014.19, MHM2014.20 and MHM2014.21.

credit_line_tsim: Gift of Su Bradfield, 2021
description_tsim: The cat eye style was introduced in the1930s, but reached the height of women’s fashion only in the 1950s. After their invention in the 1930s, cat eye glasses were becoming more prevalent. They were also known as Harlequin glasses and had thick frames with embellishments in the corners.  The 1950s was a time of shifting fashions for both men and women. With WWII firmly in the past, as well as the design stagnation caused by the Great Depression now long since over, styles were changing. Eyeglasses and sunglasses became an accessory rather than a utilitarian item people dreaded wearing, and the shape and designs of these 50s glasses themselves changed dramatically in this era. In addition to changing tastes, changing materials also made the new looks of 1950s glasses possible. Plastics created during wartime were now available to manufacturers of consumer products. Suddenly, there was an opportunity to create glasses frames in bright colours and unique shapes that were inexpensive to produce. They were also more comfortable to wear than glasses of the past since plastic is lightweight, temples curved gently around the ear, and comfortable nose pads were now standard.  From a collection of glasses formerly worn by Mrs M. Hassett (1891-1983) and her husband. The Glasses were worn from the early 1900s until 1983. They were originally obtained form optometrists in Warrnambool, Geelong, Ballarat and Melbourne, the most noted being Thomas Gaunt & Co. (Melbourne, Australia), late 19th century manufacturer and retailer of jewellery, clocks, watches and decorative items.

'This one is my granddaughters, they helping. This one is story of errpmangk-errpmangk (native fuschia) bush medicine. And all the family from Ipalala, our Outstation. Friday after work we go camping out to Rrutna (another family Outstation). And we cross the Finke River, foot walking to other side with my grandchildren and my Mum. Other side we look for this errpmangk-errpmangk near the mountain. It's grows mountainside. And teaching my grandchildren to look for other bush tucker too. After we get errpmangk-errpmangk, first I get a pot and put it on fire and put beef fat to boil. I rub errpmangk-errpmangk with a round rock, grind it, make it really smooth and put errpmangk-errpmangk powder in the pot and stir it with wooden spoon. After that my grandchildren, Mum and my cousin sisters we have lunch after doing bush medicine. We was having kangaroo tail with sweet potato. Because my Mum is getting old I want to look after my granchildren, teaching bush tucker and bush medicine. Kaltjinthintja means teaching.' description_tsim: Instrument for measuring the air capacity of the lungs.  Vitalograph was founded in 1963 when Dietmar Garbe developed a robust portable spirometer to screen coal miners for a disease called pneumoconiosis, also known as Black Lung. Dietmar Garbe was asked by the Medical Research Council Pneumoconiosis Panel to source or develop a simple, office spirometer to screen coal miners for pneumoconiosis, commonly called ‘Black Lung’. Up until this point spirometry could only be done in laboratories.  The result was ‘The Vitalograph’, from the essential features, ‘vital capacity’ and ‘graph’. Manufacture of Vitalograph Spirometers began within the old stables in the grounds of Dietmar and Margaret’s family home, Maids Moreton House.

description_tsim: Hand written letter of one folded page by Harry Brookes Allen regarding his complaint and an upcoming meeting of the Medical Society.  Harry Brookes Allen (1854–1926) became the first Australian-born professor at the University of Melbourne in 1882, when a reform of the Medical School split the foundation chair of anatomy, pathology and physiology into two, with Allen being appointed professor of anatomy and pathology, and his teacher, the foundation professor George Britton Halford (1824-1910) retaining his first love, physiology. As well as serving as dean for extensive periods, Allen took on numerous positions as a medical administrator and government advisor, perhaps most importantly playing a major part in the introduction of Melbourne’s extensive sewerage system in the late nineteenth century. Dr Ross L Jones

description_tsim: Certification of William Moore in February Term 1885 passed examination for Doctor of Medicine and Master of Medicine that he is the only graduate to hold those degrees, 23rd February 1887, signed by E. F A’Beckett , Registrar. On letterhead of The University of Mebourne. Edward Fitzhaley A’Beckett (1836-1922) was registrar, The University of Melbourne from  1864 to 1901.   William (Jerry) Moore (1859-1927), entered the University of Melbourne in 1878 he graduated M.B. in 1882 and B.S. in 1883, dux of his year. He was house surgeon at the (Royal) Melbourne Hospital in 1883-84 and afterwards demonstrator in anatomy at the university. He become the first recipient of the University of Melbourne's M.S. degree, conferred in 1885 at the same ceremony as his M.D.

Testimonial for Dr William Moore regular attendance at The Melbourne Hospital during his studentship. 5th April 1883,signed by Dr FitzGerald. Address on letterhead Lonsdale St West Melbourne.  Sir Thomas Naghten FitzGerald (1838-1908),  arrived  Melbourne in 1858. Had a private practice l in Lonsdale Street West. Honorary surgeon to the Melbourne Hospital 1860 to 1901, consulting surgeon 1902 to 1907. In 1884  he was appointed the first clinical lectureship in surgery created by the University of Melbourne at the Melbourne Hospital.
